question: Does feeding kibble vs. fresh food change my dog's thyroid needs or risks?
answer:
🟡 Moderate / ⚪ mechanistic — and yes, the diet matters a lot here: 

• IODINE: Commercial kibble is already fortified with iodine to meet AAFCO minimums, so kibble-fed dogs usually get plenty — meaning the over-supplementation risk (adding kelp on top and pushing iodine too high) is mostly a KIBBLE-fed-dog concern. The opposite is true for home-cooked or raw feeders: THEY are the ones who can fall short on iodine and may genuinely need a measured source. So 'should I add kelp?' has almost opposite answers depending on the bowl. 

• MINERAL FORM/QUALITY: Lower-quality kibble often uses cheaper, less-bioavailable synthetic mineral forms (e.g. sodium selenite for selenium, oxides for zinc) rather than the chelated/whole-food forms. Since selenium and zinc are exactly what the body uses to convert T4 into active T3, a dog on a cheap ultra-processed diet may technically 'meet the minimum' on paper while getting less usable mineral — a bigger concern on low-quality diets than on fresh, whole-food diets rich in organ meat, fish, and eggs. 

• INFLAMMATION: Most canine hypothyroidism is autoimmune, and chronic low-grade inflammation is thought to feed autoimmune processes. Ultra-processed, high-glycemic, low-quality diets carry a higher inflammatory load, so this is more of a concern for kibble/low-quality-diet dogs than for those on minimally-processed whole food (mechanistic reasoning, not proven cause-and-effect). 

Bottom line: kibble-fed dogs — watch for iodine EXCESS and cheaper mineral forms; fresh/raw-fed dogs — make sure iodine and trace minerals are actually IN the diet. Either way, don't guess iodine on a medicated dog — dose with a vet. (AAFCO iodine fortification; selenium/zinc bioavailability by form; inflammation–autoimmunity — mechanistic.)
